lines.text: This is Tesla's new Roadster, hanging almost upside down on a curved wall. No glue. No magnets. Just four fans.
At the reveal, it drove up this giant curved ramp, until the road was nearly over its head. And it stayed there.
Normally, gravity presses the tires into the road. That press is what gives them grip. Upside down, gravity pulls the car away.
So look at the back. Under the light bar, four round fans are built right into the diffuser.
They suck air out from under the car, through channels in the floor, and blow it out the back.
Skirts drop down along the sides to seal the gap, so fresh air can't rush back in underneath.
Now the air under the car is thinner than the air around it. And the air outside presses on every inch of the car.
Do the math. The floor is about four square meters. Drop the pressure under it by just one tenth, and the air pushes with over four tonnes.
Tesla's screen showed about forty-seven hundred kilos of downforce. Far more than the car weighs. So it sticks, even upside down.
And unlike a wing, fans work at any speed. Even standing still.
Race cars tried this in the seventies. The Chaparral and the Brabham fan car were so good, they got banned.
Tesla claims zero to sixty in under one second, and production in twenty twenty-eight. Tesla's own numbers, not tested yet.
Share it with your car crew in a private Orbi Space. Now you know!
